events.stdout:
usage: heartbeat --label NAME [--interval MINUTES] [--log PATH] [--until-file PATH]
                 [--max-ticks N] [--max-hours H] [-- COMMAND [ARG ...]]
       heartbeat --stop NAME
       heartbeat --list

Two shapes, and nothing else should ever be hand-written:

  report every so often   heartbeat --interval 30 --label train --log L -- <hook command>
  wait until it is done   heartbeat --label build --until-file out/result.json

  --label       name for this heartbeat, written on every line (required)
                (--name is accepted as the same flag)
  --interval    time between ticks, in MINUTES (default: 10). A bare number is
                minutes; a unit overrides it: 30s, 10m, 2h. A bare number above
                120 is refused rather than guessed at — write 10 for ten minutes,
                or 600s if you really mean seconds. (--every is accepted as the
                same flag.) It does not change how fast --until-file is noticed;
                that is checked every second either way
  --log         file to append to (default: one under the heartbeat state directory,
                whose path is printed when you arm)
  --until-file  stop cleanly once this path holds content; checked every second. It must
                NOT exist yet when you arm — an output file the job opens at the start is
                not a completion marker. (--until is accepted as the same flag)
  --max-ticks   stop after N ticks (default: unlimited)
  --max-hours   stop after H hours (default: 24; 0 disables)
  --            everything after this is the hook command, run once per tick. Optional when
                --until-file is given: with no hook each tick writes "waiting"

  --stop NAME   stop YOUR heartbeat with that label; another owner's is never reachable
  --list        every heartbeat running on this machine, yours marked "you"

Every ending says on stdout WHICH ending it was — FINISHED, NOT FINISHED, or STOPPED — so
the notification that wakes you can never make "the job is done" look like "I gave up".

The hook's exit status is recorded and never acted on. A tick happens even when the hook
fails, hangs, or writes nothing. A heartbeat's owner comes from the session environment, not
from an argument, so one agent can neither stop nor collide with another agent's heartbeat.

events.stdout:
usage: heartbeat --label NAME [--interval MINUTES] [--log PATH] [--until-file PATH]
                 [--max-ticks N] [--max-hours H] [-- COMMAND [ARG ...]]
       heartbeat --stop NAME
       heartbeat --list

Two shapes, and nothing else should ever be hand-written:

  report every so often   heartbeat --interval 30 --label train --log L -- <hook command>
  wait until it is done   heartbeat --label build --until-file out/result.json

  --label       name for this heartbeat, written on every line (required)
                (--name is accepted as the same flag)
  --interval    time between ticks, in MINUTES (default: 10). A bare number is
                minutes; a unit overrides it: 30s, 10m, 2h. A bare number above
                120 is refused rather than guessed at — write 10 for ten minutes,
                or 600s if you really mean seconds. (--every is accepted as the
                same flag.) It does not change how fast --until-file is noticed;
                that is checked every second either way
  --log         file to append to (default: one under the heartbeat state directory,
                whose path is printed when you arm)
  --until-file  stop cleanly once this path holds content; checked every second. It must
                NOT exist yet when you arm — an output file the job opens at the start is
                not a completion marker. (--until is accepted as the same flag)
  --max-ticks   stop after N ticks (default: unlimited)
  --max-hours   stop after H hours (default: 24; 0 disables)
  --            everything after this is the hook command, run once per tick. Optional when
                --until-file is given: with no hook each tick writes "waiting"

  --stop NAME   stop YOUR heartbeat with that label; another owner's is never reachable
  --list        every heartbeat running on this machine, yours marked "you"

Every ending says on stdout WHICH ending it was — FINISHED, NOT FINISHED, or STOPPED — so
the notification that wakes you can never make "the job is done" look like "I gave up".

The hook's exit status is recorded and never acted on. A tick happens even when the hook
fails, hangs, or writes nothing. A heartbeat's owner comes from the session environment, not
from an argument, so one agent can neither stop nor collide with another agent's heartbeat.

subscription-quota-check — read Codex / Claude Code subscription quota without
spending anything. Reports whether work can start now.

Usage:
  subscription-quota-check [--vendor codex|claude|both] [--json|--human] [--quiet]

Options:
  --vendor <v>   Which vendor to read. Default: both.
  --json         One JSON object on stdout (default when stdout is not a terminal).
  --human        One line per vendor on stdout (default when stdout is a terminal).
  --quiet        Suppress the stderr progress note.
  -h, --help     This text.

Exit codes:
  0  all requested vendors usable now
  1  at least one blocked by quota
  2  usage or argument error
  3  at least one unreadable (state unknown)
  4  at least one needs credentials refreshed

Verdict, per vendor and overall:
  go          the tightest window still has headroom
  short_only  usable, but the tightest window has less than the configured headroom left
  wait        blocked now; seconds_to_reset says for how long
  owner_action blocked by a workspace limit; contact the workspace owner
  unknown     could not be read, or the numbers could not be shown to be current
  needs_auth  credentials need refreshing
  n/a         not a subscription-limited session (API key / Bedrock / Vertex)

Notes:
  Reads only. This never invokes a model and never redeems a rate-limit reset credit.
  Run it when a decision needs it, or after something was actually blocked. It is not
  built to be polled: the Claude usage endpoint is itself rate limited.
  To wait for a reset, arm the `heartbeat` skill using seconds_to_reset of the BLOCKING
  window and re-run this probe in the hook — the reset instant is the server's to move,
  so only a fresh read proves a block is gone.
  This reads the credentials the two CLIs own. It does not measure accounts behind
  OPENAI_BASE_URL or on another machine.
  using the harness's own endpoint; quota describes only the CLIs.

events.stdout:
subscription-quota-check — read Codex / Claude Code subscription quota without
spending anything. Reports whether work can start now.

Usage:
  subscription-quota-check [--vendor codex|claude|both] [--json|--human] [--quiet]

Options:
  --vendor <v>   Which vendor to read. Default: both.
  --json         One JSON object on stdout (default when stdout is not a terminal).
  --human        One line per vendor on stdout (default when stdout is a terminal).
  --quiet        Suppress the stderr progress note.
  -h, --help     This text.

Exit codes:
  0  all requested vendors usable now
  1  at least one blocked by quota
  2  usage or argument error
  3  at least one unreadable (state unknown)
  4  at least one needs credentials refreshed

Verdict, per vendor and overall:
  go          the tightest window still has headroom
  short_only  usable, but the tightest window has less than the configured headroom left
  wait        blocked now; seconds_to_reset says for how long
  owner_action blocked by a workspace limit; contact the workspace owner
  unknown     could not be read, or the numbers could not be shown to be current
  needs_auth  credentials need refreshing
  n/a         not a subscription-limited session (API key / Bedrock / Vertex)

Notes:
  Reads only. This never invokes a model and never redeems a rate-limit reset credit.
  Run it when a decision needs it, or after something was actually blocked. It is not
  built to be polled: the Claude usage endpoint is itself rate limited.
  To wait for a reset, arm the `heartbeat` skill using seconds_to_reset of the BLOCKING
  window and re-run this probe in the hook — the reset instant is the server's to move,
  so only a fresh read proves a block is gone.
  This reads the credentials the two CLIs own. It does not measure accounts behind
  OPENAI_BASE_URL or on another machine.
  using the harness's own endpoint; quota describes only the CLIs.
